doc.title: Alan Raph interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Blindfold test: Don Sebesky's 'Malaguena' and the New York All-Star Band
summary: Raph identifies a Sebesky track. He explains Sebesky's career, the 1980s band, and the albums he made with him.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: That’s good. I’m going to play a little blindfold test with you.
But this is not the typical thing. This is a date that you’re on.
But I’m just curious if you’ll be able to remember it. Because I know you fellas do an awful lot of things and we’ll see if this rings a bell.
Yeah. That’s interesting. Yeah. From his “Giant Box.”
Was it from “Giant Box” or from a different album?
Album was called — gosh I didn’t write down the name of it.

Oh it was actually Don’s own band. It was Don’s all-star band, Cycles I think it was. Well Okay. Jimmy Pugh and I were the two trombones and we played mostly baritone horn in that band. Don — it’s an interesting story about Don — back in the 60s I used to do a lot of recording at — what’s his name band — Rudy VanGelder’s. And Creed Taylor used to record from there a lot. Creed had Verve Records at that time. And every now and then he’d pull some new talent — not new but unknown, relatively unknown. And he pulled in Bob James and Don Sebesky around the same time, gave them both an album, Don did “Giant Box” and Bob did a thing called “Opus 1” I believe. And Bob took off, Don didn’t. At least the way I saw it. And this is a worm’s eye view because I’m not seeing it from on top I’m just seeing it from how it happened to hit me. Bob became an international star. And Don was well known, did wonderful arrangements, was busy, but he wasn’t an international star. Now, years down the road he started this band, and this started in the 80s, around ’85. And the first band, which I think this record is, had Faddis and Soloff playing trumpets and Jimmy and I were playing trombone, Eddie Daniels was in the band, Alex Foster, Jimmy Madison played drums and Jay Leonhart played bass. It was a really good band that he called the New York All-Star Band. And it made a little bit of noise. We played some of the clubs and it kind of established Don now as a bandleader of some repute. Prior to that he was an arranger. Now he is a band leader. And he wore it well, he still does. We’ve done a few albums since. I think I’ve done all of his albums with him. The most recent is the “Joyful Noise” album, which is a superb Duke Ellington — I don’t know if you’ve heard it or not but oh God it’s good. And it’s one of the few albums that you are nervous for the whole date because it’s hard to play. It’s hard stuff to play. When you do a take and he says, “Okay that’s it” you think oh thank God, you know.
